paras: The whipping of Henry Carr was an attack on a Black businessman in Alexandria, Louisiana, who was seized at the jail door by white men on the night of August 28, 1903, given fifty lashes on his bare back, and ordered to leave. The whipping followed Carr's forcing a white man, J. C. Mosely, at gunpoint to apologize to Carr's wife. The story ran in white papers from Texas to Ohio and in two Black weeklies, one of which, the Chicago Broad Ax, presented it as a case of a man punished for protecting his wife.

Carr had kept a business in Alexandria for several years, described as a store by most reports and as "a saloon and gambling house" by a special dispatch to the San Antonio Daily Light. According to that dispatch, a young man named Mosely, who lived near Pollock, had spoken to Carr's wife "thinking she was some other colored woman," while the Broad Ax said that Mosley "had insulted Mrs. Carr." Carr then made Mosely go at the point of a gun and apologize to his wife, publicly according to a New Orleans dispatch.

When one of Mosely's friends tried to interfere, Carr reportedly threatened him with death. The San Antonio report said Carr was arrested and jailed on a charge of assault with a dangerous weapon, and the New Orleans dispatch said "the whites of Alexandria became infuriated."

As Carr was released from jail, a body of white men met him at the jail door. They gave him fifty lashes on his bare back, with a cowhide in the San Antonio account and a rawhide in the others. Carr was then told to leave "this section," which other reports gave as Alexandria or the state of Louisiana. The San Antonio report dated the whipping to the night of August 28, while the New Orleans dispatch, dated a day later, also placed it "last night."
No report of an arrest of the whippers, an investigation or Carr's later whereabouts appears in the coverage.

The earliest report, a special from Alexandria in the San Antonio Daily Light on August 30, ran under the headline "FIFTY LASHES FOR NEGRO" and called the whippers "representative white citizens" who "administered the punishment." That account alone added that Carr ran a gambling house and had served a term in a federal penitentiary for passing counterfeit money. The St. Paul Globe's New Orleans special the next day, headed "WHITES WHIP NEGRO," carried the deck "Colored Man Severely Lashed for Protecting His Wife."

In Louisiana, the Winnfield Southern Sentinel gave the case two sentences among its state news notes on September 4. A syndicated news digest that called the whippers "a mob" carried it to the Perrysburg Journal in Ohio on September 11 and, word for word, to the Cleveland Gazette, a Black weekly, on September 12, where it ran without comment.

The Chicago Broad Ax gave the fullest Black-press treatment on September 5, describing Carr as "an Afro-American" whipped by "the leading white citizens" and calling Mosley, with evident irony, "a white Christian gentleman." The paper wrote that Mosley's friends decided to whip and drive Carr from Louisiana "for protecting his wife," and drew the lesson that respectable colored women in the South had "no rights which white loafers or scoundrels who pass for gentlemen are bound to respect."

Accounts differ on what Mosely did: the San Antonio dispatch described a case of mistaken identity, while the Broad Ax called it an insult. They also differ on Carr's business, a store in most reports and a saloon and gambling house in the San Antonio account, which was also the only one to mention a criminal record.

reader.title: Whipping of Henry Carr
bases: A body of white men, not officers, whipped Carr as he left jail and ordered him to leave the town and state, with no killing reported (A1, A2, A6).

A special from Alexandria (A1) and a separate New Orleans special (A2) agree on the whipping, the fifty lashes, the order to leave and the forced apology, as do a Louisiana paper (A3) and the Chicago Broad Ax (A6).

accounts.label: Alexandria special (San Antonio Daily Light)
accounts.gist: Mosely spoke to Carr's wife 'thinking she was some other colored woman'; Carr forced an apology at gunpoint, threatened to kill when Mosely's friends tried to stop it, was jailed for assault, and was whipped by white citizens on release. Adds that Carr ran a saloon and gambling house and had served a federal term for counterfeiting.

accounts.label: New Orleans special (St. Paul Globe)
accounts.gist: A storekeeper was whipped by 'representative citizens' and ordered out of the state because he forced J. C. Mosely to apologize publicly to his wife and threatened a friend who interfered; 'the whites of Alexandria became infuriated.'

accounts.label: Black editor (Chicago Broad Ax)
accounts.gist: Mosley 'insulted Mrs. Carr'; Carr made him apologize, and Mosley's friends whipped Carr and drove him from the state 'for protecting his wife.'

accounts.label: Syndicated news digest
accounts.gist: Carr was met at the jail door 'by a mob', given fifty lashes and ordered to leave the state because he forced a white man to apologize to his wife.

framing.detail: The San Antonio report called the whippers 'representative white citizens' who 'administered the punishment' and added Carr's counterfeiting term and gambling house.
The St. Paul Globe headline 'WHITES WHIP NEGRO' with the deck 'Colored Man Severely Lashed for Protecting His Wife' put the cause in Carr's favor.
The Winnfield Southern Sentinel gave two bare sentences among Louisiana news notes.
The Perrysburg Journal ran the digest paragraph calling the whippers 'a mob'.
The Broad Ax called Mosley 'a white Christian gentleman' in irony and drew a lesson about the rights of colored women in the South.
The Cleveland Gazette ran the same digest paragraph without comment.
